ART ROOM LESSON · ART ROOM · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Colored Pencils — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces colored pencils through the card’s activity — shading a simple object — so the child discovers the flat-side trick that turns a flat drawing into a round one.

What is this?

Colored pencils are thin wooden pencils with colored cores instead of gray graphite. Sharp point for lines, flat side for shading — one tool, two personalities.

What does it mean?

Shading teaches pressure control: light touch makes light color, heavy hand makes dark. Controlling how hard you press is a fine-motor milestone hiding inside a coloring session.

What does the child need to know?

A small set of colored pencils, sharpened, and paper that is not too slick. Short pencils are actually easier for small hands than long ones.

Why this matters

Shading is a child’s first drawing vocabulary word — artists say shading to mean filling with soft color — and the sweep motion trains the same arm control as early handwriting.

What it teaches

Pressure control, wrist movement (the sweep), understanding that pictures can show roundness, and pencil grip — the tripod hold the card’s low grip encourages.

Words to learn

colored pencilsshadesweeplightdarkpressround

Say this to your child

“"Our colored pencils can do a trick! Hold it low and flat — now sweep, sweep, sweep like the wind blowing. Look! The apple is turning red from this side... and look how ROUND it looks!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the two holds: tall like a writing pencil for lines, low and flat for shading.
  2. Draw a big apple outline together — or let the child draw one.
  3. Lay the pencil almost flat and sweep along one side of the apple, light as wind.
  4. Sweep again beside the first strokes and let the color pile up softly.
  5. Compare the two sides — the swept side looks round. Say the word: shading.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a blue box holds a row of sharpened pencils standing point-up — every point the same height, ready for either hold.

Ask your child

"What happens if we press hard?" (dark color) "What about soft and slow?" (light color) "Which side of the apple is darker?" "Can you sweep like the wind?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may sweep everything now — including the carpet with an imaginary pencil — or carefully shade one object for ten quiet minutes, which is a gift, take it.

Out in the real world

Illustrators, architects and designers shade every day: the roundness on a cartoon character, the depth on a house drawing — all built from the same sweep the child just learned.

Try it together

Ramp race shading: draw a hill, shade the side the sun would hit dark and the other side light. The child has just done real light logic with a pencil.

Understanding check

Ask: "How do we hold the pencil for shading?" (low and flat) "What makes the color darker?" (pressing harder) "Point to the round side of the apple."

This lesson pairs with the Colored Pencils flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Art Room.
